newsitem.title: JAPAN: Security high for Japan nuclear waste ship arrival.
newsitem.headline: Security high for Japan nuclear waste ship arrival.

text.p: Police boats patrolled this northern Japanese port on Monday to head off protests by anti-nuclear activists against a British ship carrying nuclear waste from France.

The ship's arrival on Tuesday morning coincides with a rise in anti-nuclear sentiment since Japan's worst nuclear accident last week exposed 37 workers to radiation and revealed major safety flaws in the country's nuclear power industry.

The Pacific Teal left the French port of Cherbourg on January 13 carrying waste which initially came from Japan and was processed under a deal between the French state company Compagnie Generale des Matieres Nucleaires (COGEMA) and 10 Japanese power firms.
Under the terms of an agreement between Japan, Britain and France, spent Japanese uranium fuel is reprocessed into plutonium and the waste produced stored in Japan.
It includes radioactive material such as strontium, which has a half-life of several million years. The waste is mixed with glass and encased in 40 stainless steel canisters.

After testing for leakage of radiation, the canisters will be stored for 30 to 50 years at a special cooling facility at nearby Rokkasho village, Japan's only storage facility, and later buried at an unspecified location.
The government has not selected the final destination and residents fear they may be stuck with the toxic material.
Activists said they do not plan to stop the ship's entry to this port, about 580 km (360 miles) northeast of Tokyo, which was custom-built to handle nuclear-waste shipments.
But Greenpeace Japan officials told Reuters they might try to send small boats decked with anti-nuclear banners to escort the ship to its dock.
On the eve of the ship's arrival, there were only about 20 anti-nuclear activists camped in tents in the port's parks.
"Even though the numbers are small, after last week's accident we feel the wind is behind us in making people aware of the dangers of nuclear power," said Noriko Oyama of Greenpeace Japan.

On March 11, a fire which caused radiation to escape at the Tokaimura nuclear reprocessing facility, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, was not extinguished properly and caused an explosion hours later, exposing 37 workers to low-level radiation.

An investigation of the accident has so far revealed startling lapses in safety standards, including outdated firefighting equipment and delays in alerting both local residents and central authorities of the crisis.

Since the Tokaimura incident, two other nuclear plants, part of a 50-plant network that supplies one-third of Japan's power needs, have either shut or cut back production because of maintenance checks that found flaws in their operations.

When a first shipment of waste from France arrived in 1995, port authorities refused entry at the last minute until the central government promised in a written statement not to seek permanent burial of the toxic waste in the prefecture.
Tokyo plans eventually to ship 7,100 tonnes of spent fuel to France and Britain for reprocessing into 30 tonnes of fuel-grade plutonium, yielding 3,000 tonnes of waste.
Japanese authorities plan to move to plutonium technology to boost its self-sufficiency in energy needs to more than 50 percent by early next century.
